question: Which is better for peak performance: a short mild warm-up or a long intense warm-up?
citation: Neiva, H. P., Marques, M. C., Barbosa, T. M., Izquierdo, M., Viana, J. L., Teixeira, A. M., & Marinho, D. A. (2015). "The effects of different warm-up volumes on the 100-m swimming performance: a randomized crossover study." Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 29(11), 3026-3036. DOI 10.1519/JSC.0000000000000577 (PMID 26506059)

data.provenance: Reconstruction: no warm-up dataset on lock5stat.com/datapage3e.html. 11 paired 100-m freestyle times matching published group means/SDs (SWU 59.38+/-2.18 s, LWU 60.18+/-2.46 s; standard WU 59.29+/-1.95 s) exactly; within-swimmer pairing is synthetic with assumed r=0.50 (individual times unpublished). Documented in CSV header.
data.design: randomized crossover (paired), three warm-up volumes, 48 h apart

conclusion: Short mild warm-up (600 m) beat the long intense warm-up (1,800 m): swimmers averaged 59.38 vs 60.18 s, a 0.80 s advantage for the short warm-up, matching the paper's published inference that a long warm-up could impair performance. With n=11 and reconstructed pairing (assumed r=0.5) the conventional tests do not reach p<0.05 (paired p~0.28, Welch p~0.43); reaching significance needs r>=0.7.
